systemPrompt:
We're working in a project whose spec is compiled to .claude/reference, which is where to read it. Each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change. Follow the block at the top of the prompt you are answering; an earlier prompt's block no longer applies.

Its spec's Piton source, in ./spec, is only where edits to the spec go.

Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
instructions:
We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again.

Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791061055-FixRecurringIssue.understanding.md, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

content.content:
### Shape

#### Description

`piton build` runs in the project directory, compiling the spec and writing it out for the agents, the reference folder the harness reads included. A build runs either on its own, from a command, or ahead of other work that relies on the compiled spec.
Each build also writes the project's Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, to the fluency file in the project's data, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, whether the build succeeds or not, so the file keeps in step with the project's piton. Where the fluency can't be printed, the file is left as it was.

#### On Its Own

The Build Spec command, and Build in the palette, run a build on their own. They are unavailable while no project is open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, and while such a build is running, when the command shows a spinner and its tooltip says the spec is building. The build is listed among the [RunningActivityScope](../running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope) as "Building the spec".
When the build is over, a notification says how it went. A build that succeeds is titled "Built 1 file" or "Built N files", and lists each file written on a line of its own, never wrapped. A build that fails is titled "Build failed", with what the build reported. When `piton build` can't be run at all, the notification is titled "Could not run piton build", with why.

#### Projects

A build run on its own belongs to the project it started in, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, and carries on when switching to another project. The command shows it running only while that project is on screen; another project can build at the same time. When it is over while another project is on screen, its notification's title ends with the name of the project it built, such as "Built 3 files in my-project".

#### Ahead Of Work

A build ahead of other work runs when that work actually starts, not when it is asked for, and shows as a step of that work until it is over. It isn't listed among the running activity on its own, since the work it leads is.
A build that fails, or can't be run, never stops the work that follows, since that work may be what fixes the spec, or can go on with the compiled spec as it was. The work says the build failed, so the compiled spec may be out of date, with what the build reported.

#### After Spec Work

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up, runs in a container with no code location, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, so any build it runs there writes only the reference it can see. Once its run is over, however it ended, done, failed, or cancelled, a build runs on the host, as one ahead of work does, so the host's compiled reference, and the shape guidance written into the code location, are those of the spec as the run left it. It runs before the task shows as finished, the task showing "Building" meanwhile, and then the task finishes in the state its run ended in. A build that fails, or can't be ru

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope

export scope ContainerEnvironmentScope:
    concept: {ContainerEnvironmentConcept}

concept ContainerEnvironmentConcept:
    pitch:
        A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works
        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the
        only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always
        run on the host, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, with their
        protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always
        run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's
        installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and
        runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

    podmanAccess:
        Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is
        running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container
        for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is
        missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its
        service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because
        of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or
        any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed.
        The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and
        failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it
        prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or
        question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run
        because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written,
        what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead.
        The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for
        that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that
        the build failed.

    image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The
        build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as
        `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built
        against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which
        command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't
        run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run
        `piton build` to check its work.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what
        its runs in a container need, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in
        the container, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, on every platform, each location given
        at its place relative to the project directory under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`,
        and the run works in `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`. So a harness that keys its
        sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them
        again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What
        each kind of run is given, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} names
        the locations, follows.

        spec:
            A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the
            spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the
            harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can
            run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which
            holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write,
            for the same reason; the fluency file, read only;
            piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file,
            read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty
            scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes
            with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it
            places the shape's guidance in.

        question:
            A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec
            location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read
            only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container. Nothing is
            writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions
            folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location
            holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither
            is hidden from the question by the other.

        Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read
        and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.

        Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the
        user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the
        project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code
        location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without
        the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless
        the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both
        the code location and the spec location.

        A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history
        folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file
        has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just
        before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not
        written yet is.

    paths:
        On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is
        mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project
        directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec
        in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its
        understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls
        touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with
        `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as
        `/workspace-old`. A path
        that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and
        opens nothing.

    volumes:
        The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings,
        ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness
        keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every
        project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing
        one costs only a login.

        The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in
        the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and
        `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own
        conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its
        sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never
        `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another
        conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before
        the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs,
        restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

        Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
        context: the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
        can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried
        over; each conversation starts fresh.

    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

    specBuild:
        A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work
        in the refreshed reference, and that build succeeds whenever the spec
        is sound: it owns the reference files it finds, through the
        manifest in the mounted `.piton` directory, and places the shape's
        guidance in the scratch directory standing in for the code location,
        where it goes nowhere. A build there that fails fails only because of
        the spec, never because of what the container leaves out, so its
        errors are the run's own to fix. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over,
        however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as
        the @{SpecBuildScope} says, so the host's reference and shape guidance
        are those of the spec as the run left it.

use /lib
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/no-project import NoProjectStateScope
from /scope/open-projects import OpenProjectsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/running-activity import RunningActivityScope

export scope SpecBuildScope:
    concept: {SpecBuildConcept}

concept SpecBuildConcept:
    pitch:
        Brings the project's compiled spec up to date, so what the harness
        reads of the spec is what the spec says now.

    shape: {SpecBuildShape}

shape SpecBuildShape:
    description:
        `piton build` runs in the project directory, compiling the spec and
        writing it out for the agents, the reference folder the harness reads
        included. A build runs either on its own, from a command, or ahead of
        other work that relies on the compiled spec.

        Each build also writes the project's Piton fluency, what
        `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, to the fluency file in the
        project's data, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, whether the
        build succeeds or not, so the file keeps in step with the project's
        piton. Where the fluency can't be printed, the file is left as it
        was.

    onItsOwn:
        The Build Spec command, and Build in the palette, run a build on their
        own. They are unavailable while no project is open, as the
        @{NoProjectStateScope} says, and while such a build is running, when the
        command shows a spinner and its tooltip says the spec is building. The
        build is listed among the @{RunningActivityScope} as
        "Building the spec".

        When the build is over, a notification says how it went. A build that
        succeeds is titled "Built 1 file" or "Built N files", and lists each
        file written on a line of its own, never wrapped. A build that fails is
        titled "Build failed", with what the build reported. When
        `piton build` can't be run at all, the notification is titled
        "Could not run piton build", with why.

    projects:
        A build run on its own belongs to the project it started in, as the
        @{OpenProjectsScope} says, and carries on when switching to another
        project. The command shows it running only while that project is on
        screen; another project can build at the same time. When it is over
        while another project is on screen, its notification's title ends with
        the name of the project it built, such as "Built 3 files in my-project".

    aheadOfWork:
        A build ahead of other work runs when that work actually starts, not
        when it is asked for, and shows as a step of that work until it is
        over. It isn't listed among the running activity on its own, since the
        work it leads is.

        A build that fails, or can't be run, never stops the work that follows,
        since that work may be what fixes the spec, or can go on with the
        compiled spec as it was. The work says the build failed, so the compiled
        spec may be out of date, with what the build reported.

    afterSpecWork:
        A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up, runs in a
        container with no code location, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope}
        says, so any build it runs there writes only the reference it can see.
        Once its run is over, however it ended, done, failed, or cancelled, a
        build runs on the host, as one ahead of work does, so the host's
        compiled reference, and the shape guidance written into the code
        location, are those of the spec as the run left it. It runs before the
        task shows as finished, the task showing "Building" meanwhile, and
        then the task finishes in the state its run ended in. A build that
        fails, or can't be run, never changes that state: the task's output
        ends with a passive notice saying the build failed, with what it
        reported. The chain's next step is sent only once it is over.

I've specced a fix so this error stops appearing. `piton check` reports no problems, both files are formatted, `piton build` succeeds, and I confirmed the new sections in the refreshed reference.

**Why it keeps happening:** `piton build` refuses to overwrite any reference file its manifest (`.piton/manifest.json`) doesn't list. There are two ways the manifest falls out of step with `.claude/reference`:

- **Spec runs don't get the real manifest.** In this run, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/.piton` is a temporary filesystem, not the project's own `.piton` folder. A build inside the container writes its manifest there, and it's thrown away with the container.
